title: African resistance against colonial expansion
competency: Evaluate African responses to colonialism: Samori Toure, the Ashanti, Urabi Pasha, the Mahdists and Maji-Maji, and why most resistance failed.

en.text: Africans did not welcome the uninvited Europeans. Colonizers used fake treaties and, when these failed, force; Africans replied both peacefully and violently to defend their sovereignty, and resisted in almost every region. Most resistance failed because it was poorly organized, Europeans had better training and firearms, and Europeans used Africans against fellow Africans. The only successful case was Ethiopia: Menelik II defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and the colonial powers recognized Ethiopia's independence.

ideas.name: Samori Toure and the Wassoulou Empire

en.text: Samori Toure (c. 1828–1900), a Muslim leader of the Mandinka, founded the Wassoulou Empire in today's Guinea, with its capital at Bissandugu. He built a well-trained army of infantry and cavalry, paid for by the Bure gold mines and armed with guns bought through Freetown. He beat the French in 1882 and drove them from Bure in 1885, but from 1891 the French advanced, took his capital, and the British stopped selling him guns. He was captured on 29 September 1898, exiled to Gabon, and died there on 2 June 1900.

en.text: The Ashanti (Asante), Akan-speaking people of today's Ghana, built a state around Kumasi in the late 1600s. Osei Tutu (Asantehene 1701–1717) and his priest Komfo Anokye united the chiefdoms, created the Golden Stool and the Odwira festival, and made gold dust the currency. By the early 1800s Ashanti exported enslaved people for firearms and was at war from 1790 to 1896. It resisted Britain from 1823 to 1873; Britain captured Kumasi in 1874, occupied it again in 1896, crushed the 1900 uprising and annexed Ashanti to the Gold Coast in 1902.

ideas.name: Urabi Pasha in Egypt and the Mahdists in Sudan

en.text: In Egypt, army officer Ahmed Urabi joined an 1879 mutiny that grew into the 1881–82 revolt against Khedive Tewfik and Anglo-French control; after riots in Alexandria in 1882, Britain bombarded the city, occupied Egypt and exiled Urabi to Ceylon. It was the first Egyptian nationalist movement. In Sudan, Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the Mahdi in 1881, won at Aba (1881) and Kordofan (1883), and took Khartoum in 1885, killing Gordon. His successor Khalifa Abdullah ruled until Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army won at Omdurman in 1898; Sudan became the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium.

en.text: The Maji-Maji Rebellion broke out in July 1905 in the Matumbi hills, in the hinterland of Kilwa in German Tanganyika, because of heavy taxes and forced labour on cotton farms. It was spontaneous, with no central leadership, but it united the peoples of southern Tanzania through belief in maji, a magic water said to turn bullets into water. Ethnic differences, machine-guns, German reinforcements and a scorched-earth policy broke it; the Ngoni were defeated in 1907 and famine followed. It inspired the nationalists who won independence in the early 1960s.

notes.text: Spellings: the book prints "Mahadist/Mahaddists" (standard: Mahdist), "Samori Touri" (Samori Toure), "Cot d' Ivoire" (Côte d'Ivoire), "Sera Leone" (Sierra Leone), "Kitchner" (Kitchener), "Dar es Selam" (Dar es Salaam), "perused" (pursued), "farma" (farms). The lesson uses the standard forms.

Samori: p.36 misprints his death as 2 June 1990 (correct: 1900, as on p.34). On 29 September 1898 he was captured (as p.34 says), not "surrendered". "Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone since 1876" is read as "imported firearms via Freetown from 1876". The capital is Bissandugu (p.36 "Bissangudu"); most histories date its fall to April 1891, the book June 1892 — the lesson says 1891–1892.

Ashanti: the British occupied Kumasi and exiled Asantehene Prempeh I in 1896 (book: 1897, p.36 and p.37); the 1900 uprising (War of the Golden Stool) came after that exile. p.37 "In the 18th century" should be 17th; by then the Dutch and English, not the Portuguese, were the most active Europeans on the Gold Coast.
Urabi: the 1881–82 revolt was against Khedive Tewfik (p.38 wrongly says "Khedive Ismael Pasha", who was deposed in 1879). The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium was formally set up in January 1899.
Added (marked): the Ethiopian link — Emperor Yohannes IV was killed fighting the Mahdists at Metemma (March 1889). The Adwa hook reasoning (unity and good weapons) is added.
